Now the Manner of the Medullary Oils insinuating isles in a Bone, and its being dispensed to all the Parts of it, is this: Ir first passes, being Liquid ( sit all is while the Animal is alive) out of the Cavity, through the transverse Pores of the first internal Lamine, and not having Pores of the same kind dire tly subjacent in the next Place to transmit it towards the outside of the Bone, it flows into the Longittidinal ones formed between these two ( the first and second) Plates, and being carried along in them till it find some transverse Pores in'the second Plate, it passes through these which when it has done, it is obliged again to alter its Course, to run into and flow along the streight Pores between the second and third Lamina. Thus it passes fe and between the Places succus on till ic has made its way to the External ate. . Thus the Medullary Oil is dispensed in all the Bones. to those Plates which are contiguous, and have no intermediate Cavities to-entertain any Me - dullary'Glands of their: own: But where the Plates fland at some distance ( as'they do in such - Bones as have not any great Cavity) there are the mall Caverns ( abovementioned) which are capa ble of containing some Medullary Glands, from whence the Plates have more immediately, and without the former Method of Conveyance, the Benefit of the Marrow. Y He divides the Blood-Vessels of the Bones into Nutritious and Medullary. " The most considerable of the Nutritious enter at the ends of the Bone, viz. the Artery at one End, and the Veins at the other. The A / medullary commonly enter the Sides of the Bones ( and that obliquely, as the Ureters do the Bladder) both by one Foramen. There arena Nerves that are insert d into'them ( except into the Teeth) but these only run through the Fericflewm that invests them.; Some, Bones have Cavities in them, as Os Humeri, ad Femoris, the Una and Radius, Tibia and Fibula, the Bones of the Metacarpus and Metatarsus, of the Fingers and Toes, and of the Os Hyoides; to which may be added, the lower Jaws; though the Cavity compared with the Magnitude of the Bone, hardly deserves to be stile large: Besides these large Cavities which are in the Isle of the Bones, there are lesser Cells or Caverns in their Substance, which are found in all the Bones, even those which have large Cavity. But of these before, when we spoke of the Distribution of the Marrow. Besides the large Cavities and Caverns in theIn - side or Substance of the Bones, most have Superficial Cavities or Sinus's which Dr. Havers distinguishes into Suki or Furrows ( which are the long ones) and Pits, as he calls the shorter ones. they have besides, Ho / es for the Nuiritious and Medullary Vessels, as'was but just now observed. On the outside of the Bones there are also to be observed, their Prominences or Protuberances, of which there be two kinds; for it is either a continued part ofthe Bone jetting manifestly above its plain Superficies, for the more saiesiions Insertion of the Muscles, &c. and is called Aporhyyis, a Process; or else it is like an additional Bone grow - ing to another by simple and immediate Contiguity, ( and generally fott and more us than it) and is called Epithyfis, an Appendage. If the Protuberance of the Bone be round, iris called its Capuit; under which is the Cervix, as in the upper end of the Thigh-bone: If it be flat, it is called Condylus if sharp, Corone, from the Similitude they have to other things, as Sty / oides, Coracotdes. Their Ujes are many; for they serve, 1. For the Fermitude and Sustentation of the Body, like Beams and Pillars in Houses. 2. For a Defence to. some Parts; so the Skull defends th Brain, the Ribs the Parts contained in the Breast.. 3. For Progression or Walking, of which they with the Muscles are the only Instruments. 4. They give Shape to the Parts of the Body. These are their general Ules as to their particular Uses, those will be Shewn as we describe them severally.

And to the same Purpose it is, that the Webs of some Spiders, by being spun very fine, have appeared co een, as some have observed; and that the coloured Fibres of some Silks, by varying the Position of the E do vary their Colour: Also the Colours of Silks, Cloaths, and other Substances which Water or Oyl can intimately penetrate, become more faint and ob ure by being immerged in these Liquors, and recover their Vigor again by drying, much after the manner of the thin Bodies mentioned in the both and 12 th Observations. propositions.c: PROPOSITIONS. 1. The Sun's Light consists of Rays differing by indefinite Degrees of Refrangibility. 2. Rays which differ in Refrangibility, when parted from one another, do proportionably differ in the Colours which they exhibit. These two: Propositions are Matter of Fa t. Y bodessy 3. There are as sean, Simple or Homogeneal Colours, as Degrees of Refrangibility; for to every Degree of Refrangibility belongs a different Colour, by Prop. 2. And that Colour is: Simple, by Def. 1. and 3.; fs 4. Whiteness, in all refle ts like that of the Sun's immediate Light, and of the usual Objects of our Senses, cannot. be compounded of two simple Colours alone; for such a Composition: must be made by Rays that have only two Degrees of Re frangibility, by Def. 1, and 3.. And therefore it cannot be like that of the Sun's Light, by Prop. 1. Nor for the same Reason, like that ot ordinary White Obje & s. g-Whiteness, inallrefpe ts like that of the Sun's immediate Light, cannot be compounded of Simple Colours, without an indefinite Variety of them: For to such a Composition there are required Rays endued with all the indefinite Degrees of Refrangibility, by Prop. 1. And those infer as many Simple Colours, by Def. 1, and 3. and Prop, 2, and 3.: 6. The Rays of Light do not a & on one another, in passing through the same Medium. 7. The Rays of Light suffer not any Change of their isles from Refra ion., or afterwards from the adjacent quiet Meds um. These two Propositions are manifest de facto in Homogeneal Light; whose Colour and Refrangi ability is not at all changeable, either by Refraction, or by Con termination of the quiet Medium. And as for Heerageneal Light, ivis but an Aggre a of several forts of Homogeneal Light; no one sort of which suffers any more Alteration than if it were alone, because the Rays a not upon one another, by Prop. 6. and therefore the Aggregate can suffer none. 9. There can no Homogeneal Colours be reduced. out of Light by Refraction, which are not. commit init before; because, by Prop. 7, and 8. Refratti - On changeth not the Qualities of the Rays, but only separates, those which have divers Qualities, by means of their different Refrangibility. 1 10. The Sun's Light is an Aggregate of an inde finite Variety of Homogeneal Colours, by Prop, 1, 3, and. And hence itis, that Homogeneal Colours may be called Primitive or. Original. That Light is a Body, Mr. Molyneux, in his Dit tricks, proves from the various Properties of it; s, I. By the Affection of its being Refracted, tis ma - nifeft, that Light, in its Passage through this and. t'other Diaphanous Body, does find a ferent Re ance. Now " tis unconceivable how any. but Body should suffer Resistance; but we may conceive sibieias schathinTihitaintatidiiictaatl " EeliGs weive. the Resistance that Light suffers in its Passage through different Di. Bodies to: proceed from the Medium hindering the Dijfujiow or Difi ri - bastion of Light through more of the Parts of this Medium, and consequently it may be said to. be dess illuminable: For from the Nature of it, Light endeavours to d: souse iv self: And the'contrary, by - how much Light does: more equally or uniformly affe the Parts of the Medium, which it enlightens; or by how much it communicates its Exergy to more of the Particles of the enlightened Space, that Medium may be said to be by so'much the more illume - table, or less to resist the Progress of Light. Whence it is, that by how miuchrthe affected Parts of the Medium are more solid and small, and admit between them the / e / s Space for any other Heterogeneozs Matter that suffers not by Light, by so much the Medium is said to be more enlightened. And tis certain, That Resistance must proceed froth the Conta of two Bodies; and Contad, either Ad ive or Pressive, belongs only to Body. The Second Property that confirms Light to be a Body, and a Body moved or thrust forward, is, That it requires Zine to pass from one Place to another, and does it not in an Jn / take, but is only of all Motions the guicke / t: For Mr. Romer has demonstrated, beyond all Contra di tion, from the Observations of the Immerfiows and Emerfions of the Satellites of Jupiter, That Light requires the Time of one Second to move the Space of 3000 Leagues, or 9000 Miles, which is near the Earth's Diameter; as may be seen inthe Four nal des Spavans, 1676. Decemb. 7. Philosophical Transactions, Nam. 136. Or Sir [ fa ae Newton's Philof. Natur. Math, Lib. t. Se hol. Prop. 96. where tis asserted, That Light requires about 10 Minutes Time to come fromthe Sz to the Earth: Avid tis most evident, without this Allowance for the Time spent in Light's Motion, the Appearances of the Satellites, Eclipses, and Emerfions, are not to ee by any Excentricity, or other Hypothesis. A Third Proof that Light is a Body, is, That it cannot by any Art or Contrivance whatsoever, be increas'd or dieninifb'd that is to fay, we cannot magnify ( for Instance) the Light of the Sum, or a Candle, no more than we can magnify a Cubick Inch of Gold, or make it more than a Cubick Inch: for whenever we fee Light increased, tis by robbing it of some other Part of the Medium of. its Light, or by bringing the Light that naturally should have been diffused through some other Part, to the more enlightened Place: Thus, for Instance, in a Burning-Glass, by which the Light of the Sum is highly increased in its Focus, or Burning-Point, we are first to confider, That in this Flows the Image of the Sun is J rate as being the distinct Base of the Glass: And Secondly, We may observe all round about this bright Spot of the Sun's Image, there is cast the strong Shadow of the whole Breadth of the Burning-Glass: For all the Rays from the Sun, that would have fallen on this broad shaded Space, erenow brought together, and crowded close in this bright Spot, there raising a vigorous Light and violent Heat. his is abundantly confirmed by an easy Experiment: For cover all the Burning-Glass, except one small round Space in its Middle, just the Bigness of the bright burning Spor in its Focus; and though there be a thaded Space round the bright Speck, as before, yet we shall not be sensible of any Increase either of Light ot Heat; which plainly thews, That this Increase of Light ( when the Glass is all bare) proceeds from the crowding together of those Rays that would have fallen on the reft of the Glass; and which ( were not the Glass) interposed) would have fallen on, the thaded Space round about the bright Speck.: here seems but. one Objedion againt what is here laid down; and that is, That Light is increas ed by Reflexion, without depriving any Place of the Light it would, otherwise receive; or without bringing to the enlightened Part any Light that would: otherwise escape it, or never come at it. But if we confider the Matter more attentively, we shall find it otherwise: For suppose an Hole ot a Foot Square in the Side of a. Chamber, and that a Candle were placed close to, and just before the Middle of this Hole; there is. but half this Candle that new enlightens this Room, the other half of its Rays proceeding dire tly out at the Hole: Let now a Looking-Glass be placed so, as just to fill wp this Hole; the Rays which before would have gone out at the Hole, are now refle ted into the Room; so that the Hemisphere without the Chamber, which, was enlightened whilst the Hole continued open, is now robbed of its Light; and all this Light is now refle ed into its Room, whereby the aver / e Side of the Flame is made to enlighten, as well as. the Side directly exposed to the Chamber, What is said of this Cafe, may be accommodated to all: For so a Looking-Glass lying horizontally, and refle ting the Sun-beams to the Cieling of the Room, does plainly hinder the dire Progress of the Rays to some other Part, and consequently robs that Part of its Light. This is evident, by supposing an Hole behind the Glass, as in the former Cafe. 7 From whence tis manifest, how vainly they attempt, who offer at increasing Light uniformly, that is, equally throughout the whole Sphere of a Luminous Body, or Radiating Point: Such are the Pretences of those that would persuade the World of Contrivances for making the small Flame of a Lamp enlighten strongly a whole Chapel, Hall, or Court, by being hung up in the midst thereof: For these things are impossible to be effected in Nature, and: they had as well, pretend to create Light; for there is no other way of increasing it, unless by robbing another Place of its Light, and then tis not uniformly increased. We have a very sensible Instance of this inthe mew-invented Lanthorns, now much used in London, which, by the Con - vex-Glasses in their Sides, do strongly throw those Rays along the Walks of the Patlengers, which would otherwise ( were the Glasses away, and the round Holes left open) be pent on Parts of the Streets not frequented; whereby the un trodden Parts of the Streets are robbed of their Light, more strongly to supply and enlighten the Paths where the Light is requisite. The Intenseness of Light ( as also of Heat) is always proportionable to the Density of the Rays that produce it: And that Density always is in all Places, or stall Distances from the Center of Radiation, as the Squares of such Distances reciprocally: See eae In the French Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Sciences, there is an Account of a New Theory of Light, which is started by M. Malebranche: He thinks Light and Colours do arise from Vibrations of the insensible Parts of Bodies, as Sounds do: And therefore, according to the Degree of the Rapidity of the Motion of the Parts of a Luminous Body, it will appear enlightened more or less; and in lesser Degrees of such vibrating Motion, it will appear not Luminous, butoffachandfach Colours: see Vol. Il.; 3 LIKE

parvagum.c: PAR Vagum, a pair of Nerves arising below the Auditory ones, from the Sides of the Medulla Oblongata, behind the ProcefJus Annularis, by several Threads which join together, and go out by the same Hole that the Sinus Laterals discharge themselves in to the Fugulares. It is joined by a Branch of the Nero us Spinalis, or Accessorius Willis, and by a mall Branch of the Portio Dura: Immediately after ix comes out of the Skull, it gives a mall Branch to the Larynx, as it goes down the Neck, above the Intercostal Nerve, by the Sides of the Internal Carotide. At the Axillary Artery it casts back the Re currant Nerves, of which the Right embraces the Axillary Artery, and the Left the Aorta, These two Branches ascend on each Side of the Trachea, Afpera Arteria, to the Larynx, where they are pent on the Muscles of the Larynx and Membranes of the Trachea. This Pair, after it has entred the Cavity of the Thorax, fends our several Branches to the Pericardium, Heart, Lungs, and Concave side of the Liver. This pair of Nerves was formerly accounted the Sixth, bur is now usually reckoned the Eighth,. at a; There is a notable Fibre, or rather Nerve, coining from the Spinal Marrow, about the Sixth or Seventh Vertebra of the Neck, which is so joined to this Par Vagum, as if they grew into one Nerve; being covered with ir, with the same Coat, from the Dura mater, but appears diftin & when that is taken, off. " This Nerve they call the Accessory Nerve, which runs'to the Muscles of the Neck and Shoulder-Blade.;: Ours the Trunks of this Eighth Pair spring two N ryes that they call the Recur rin Nerves; the Right of which rises higher, and winds about the Axillary Artery; the Left springs lower, and twisting about the Trunk of the descending Aorta, fecurrs or return back from thence. Ps Willis thinks this Re currant Nerve to be re ally a distinct one from the very Original, ro be no Branch of the Par Vagum, but only is included in the same Coat or Cover with it, for Safery and Convenience of Passage. About the first and second Rib this Pair hath ind of Plexus. os Knot, which is called Plexus Cardiacus, because it fends out Twigs which go to the Heart and its Appendages.. -

pension.c: PENSION, that which in the two Temples is called a Parliament, and in Lincolns-Inn a Council, is in Grays-Inn termed a Pension; that is, an Assembly of the Members of the Society, to consult of the Affairs of the House. Also in the Inns of Court, Pensions are certain annual, Payments of each Member to the House, for certain Occa - sions... /
PENSION 77 rit, when a Pension Writ is once issued, none sued thereby in the Inns of Court shall be discharged, or permitted to come. into Commons, till all Duties be paid.

pentapotes.c: PENTAPOTES, ( in Grammar) are such de fi - tremities, terminate in the supe: cent Nouns as have but five Cafes, as Nemo.

perambulation.c: PERAMBULATION f the Foreft, is the Surveying or Walking about the Forest, or the Limits of it, by Justices, or other Officers thereto appointed, to fer down the Metes and Bounds thereof, and what is within the Foreft, and what without.:

perambulatione.c: PERAMBULATIONE facienda, is a Writ that is sued out by two or more Lords of Mannors lying near one another, and consent ing to have their Bounds severally known, It is directed to the Sheriff, commanding him to rake Perambulation, and fer down their certain Limits.

perambulator.c: PERAMBULATOR, or Walking-wheel, is an Engine made of Wood or Iron, commonly half a Pole in Circumference, with a Movement, and a Face divided like a Clock, with a long Rod of Tron or Steel, that goes from the Centre of rhe Wheel to the Work: There are also two Hands, which ( as you drive the Wheel before you) count the Revolution; and from the Composition of the Movement, and by the Division on the Face, shew how tinny Yards, Poles, Furlongs, and Miles you go. The Use of this Instrument is to measure Roads, Rivers, and all Level Lands, with great Expedition.

perception.c: PERCEPTION, is the clear and diftin t Apprehension of any Object offered to us, without forming any Judgment concerning them.

perchameasure.c: PERCH, a Measure by our Statute-Law, of x 6 Foot and halfen Length. See Pole.

perdonatio.c: PERDONATIO utlagaria, is a Pardon for of the third Bone of each Finger.

per.c: PER tion and Fore-part The Tendons of this Muscle running through those of the perforated, is a no less useful than stupendous Artifice in Nature. For to the end the Fingers ( like so many Leavers) should be bended with great Force, it is absolutely necessary the strongest Muscle should be inferred nearest-their Extremities, and farthest from their Fuleimenta the Ossa Metacarpi: But in Regard every Internode should be attended with a particular Muscle, the better to accommodate them to various Imploy - ments, and the Origination of the Superior or Perforatus is consi tied to the Apex of the Internal Extuberance ofthe Os Humers, and upper part of the Radius only; wherefore could not be a fit Instrument for so strenuous an Action, and that not only in Regard'to its Magnitude, but by the Approach of its rwoExtreams when the Cubit or Carpus are bended; both which would be no small Impediments in divers Actions; it'stherefore necessary it should be employed in the Motions of j the second Internodes: But since these superior Tendons'would be hereby liable to interrupt the inferior in their right Progress to the Extremities of the Fingers; ir seems an Argument of great Counsel in transmitting the latter thro the Sis - fares of each of the former, whereby the Actions of both are not only diftin tly performed, and the. Exiremitles of the Fingers attended with the largest Muscle, ( whose Origin is below the Os Humeri, wherefore its Extreams cannot aj in the Flexion of the Cubit,) but theif Moti otis are preserved, tho the superior Muscle is totally, divided; which indeed is a provident Contrivance ofthe Author of Nature, and is in ie self sufficient to excite our Admiration,:

perforansamusele.c: PERFORANS, a Musele of the lesser Toes 5 so called, because its Tendons run thro the Fissures in the Tendons of the Mufculus perforatus pedis: It is also called Flexor tertii Internodii Di - Sit orum pedis, from its use. It hath ana cure fleshy Origination from the back part of the Tibia, immediately under the Mufewlus fub popliteus, having double Orders Fibres united ina middle Tendon like the Flexor pollicis longus, but ceafeth to be fleshy sit passeth behind the Malleolus inter nus, and running ina Channel over the internal part of the Os Calc s, under it, imbanking Ligaments in half its progress thro the Sole of the Foot; it is divided into four Tendons, which march thro the perforations of the Tendons ofthe perforatus pedis, and are inserted to the third Bone t of every lesser T ie oe.

perforatus.c: PERFORATUS, isa Muscle belonging'to the. him who for Contempts. in not coming to the King's Court, is out - law'd, and afterwards of his own Accord, yieldeth himself to Prison.

peremptoryinlaw.c: PEREMPTORY, in Law, signifies a final and determinate Act, without Hope of renewing or altering. 4

perfectnumbers.c: PERFECT Numbers, are such whose aliquot or even Parts, join'd together, will exactly return the whole Number, as 6, 28, &c. For of 6, the half is 3, the third part 2, and the sixth Part 1, which added together, make 6; and it hath no mere aliquot Parts in whole Numbers: So 28, which has these Parts, viz. 14, 7, 4, 2, and 1, exactly return 28; which therefore is a versed) Number, whereof there is but ten between One and One Million of Millions. - Mi PERFORANS, is a Muscle of the Fingers, so) ah called, because its Tendons run thro those'of the Perforaeus; it's also call'd profundus, stom its Sir aa - Mt tion: and tertii Internodit Digitorum Flexor, stom its use, It rifeth fleshy from near two Thirds of the Siiperior and Fore-part of the Ulna, as also) from the, Ligathent between the last named Bone! and the Radius; and becoming a large thick bel - lied Muscle, grows outwardly tendinous, before is passes over the Pronator Radii Quadratus, and is divided into'four round Tend oris, Which match 1 under those of the perforated Muscle, beneath the Ligamentum tranfverfale; from each of these dex dons the Mu / eli Lumbricales are said'to arise; after which they pass thro " the Fissures of those of the! perforated Muscles, and proceeding'o er'their Ex - somes so many roundish 1 dons, which are included in their proper vilineal or Mix'd. tum Tranfverfale Carpi thro the Palm; near the first Internode of the Fingers each Tendon is divided to admit those of the Perforated Muscle thro them; then joining and subdividing again immediately before they are inserted to the Superior part of the second Bone of each Finger.

perforatuspedis.c: PERFORATUS Pedis, isa Muscle of the lesser Toes; so called, because irs Tendons are Perforated like those of the Fingers. It is also called, Flexor secundi Internodii Digitorum Pedis, from its Use; and Sublimis from its Situation. It springeth from the Inferior and Internal part of the Os Calcis, between the Muse uli Abduflores of the Greater-and lesser Toes, dilating it self to Fleshy Belly, After ir hath passed the Middle of the Planta Pedis, it is divided into four Flefliy Portions, which becoming so many Tendons, are divided near their Terminations, to admit the Tendons of the Perforans to pa s thro them to their Insertions: These being united again, pass underneath them to their Implanrations at the upper Part of the second Bone of each lesser Toe.

perforated.c: PERFORATED, i.. bored thro, The Armorifts uf it to express the passing or pene tra ting of one Ordinary ( in part) thro another; as thus: He beareth Or, bend Ermine Perforated thro a Chevron Gules. But when there is only a Hole made thro the Ordinary, and nothing in it to fillet up, they call it Piercing.

periamma.c: PERIAMMA, calledalfoPeriapta, is medicine, which being tied about the Neck, is believed to expel Diseases, e specially the Plague. See Happen / 2.

pericarpium.c: PERICARPIUM, is a Medicine applied to the Wrifts, ro cure an Ague, c.

pericardium.c: PERICARDIUM, is a double Membrane which surrounds the whole Substance of the heart, - and contains a te: ed to Moisten, Lubricate, and, " as some fay, to Re frigate the Heart: It hath five Holes, according to the Number of Vessels which go out of the Heart. It adheres to the Mediastinum at the Basis, and arte Mucro to the Centre, or Nervous Part of the Diaphragma,

pericarnium.c: PERICARNIUM, is a Membrane which infolds the Skull, feared next to the Periostium, covering the whole Skull, except just where the Temporal Muscles lie. It is of exquisite Sense; and causes intolerable Pain when the Temporal Muscle is wounded.:

periacl.c: PERIACL, are those Inhabitants of the Earth who live under the same Parallels, but under opposite Semi-circles of the Meridian, whence they have the same Seasons of the Year, viz. Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter, - at the very same Time, as also the same Length of Days and Nights; for it is inthe same Climate, and tan equal Distance from the Equator: But the Changes of Noon and Midnight, are alternate one to " the other.

perig.c: PERIG hon, or Perigeum, is'a Point in the Heavens, wherein a Planet is said ro be in its nearest Distance possibly from the Earth.

perihelion.c: PERIHELION, is rhat point of a Planet's Orbit, wherein it is nearest to the Sun.

perimeter.c: PERIMETER, is the Compass or Sum of all the Sides which bound any Figure, whether Rec - they Studied or Taught were called, ed

perindevalve.c: PERINDE Valve, 2 Term belonging to; the Ecclesiastical Law, signifying a Di peniation grant - ed to. a Clerk, that being defective in his Capa - city to a Benefice, or other Ecclesiastical Function, is de Fa o admitted to it: And it hath the Appellation from the Words, which make. the Faculty as effectual to the Party dispensed. with, axis he had been actually capable of the Thing for which he is dispensed with at the Time of his Admission. Iris called a Writ. ne ye

perineum.c: PERINEUM, is the Ligament ous Seam betwixt the Scrotum and the Fundament.

period.c: PERIOD, isa Full-stop at the End of any Sentence. A Period in Numbers, is a Distinction made by a Point or Comma after every sixth Place or Figure; and ir is used in Numeration for the reader distinguishing and naming the several Figures or Places: Which) how to do, fee under Numeration.)

periodinchronology.c: PERIOD, in Chronology, signifies a Revolution of a certain Number of Years; as the Metonick Period, the Julian Period, and the Calippick Period:; Which see in their proper places.

periodical.c: PERIODICAL, is the Term for whatever performs its Motion, Course, or Revolution, regularly, so as to return again, and to dispatch it always in the same Period or Space of Time, Thus the Periodical Motion of the Moon, is that whereby she finishes her Course round about the Earth in a Month; and this is 27 Days, 7 Hours, 45 Minutes; and is called, The Moon's:

periodicalmonth.c: PERIODICAL Month; which is the Space of Time that the Moon finishes her. Revolution in.

periodussanguinis.c: PERIODUS Sanguinis, is'a continued Circulation of the Blood thro the Body; which is thus made: The Blood is carried out of the Arteries by Fibres, either of the Fieth or of the Entrails, or the Membranous Parts, faith Blanchard; - but itis cerceiliir is by a Capillary Arteries continued with the like small Veins into the Mouth of the greater Veins, and implanted in them, as we fee, many other little Channels in the Veins; so the Blood, passing thro these ont of the Arteries, is presently sent to the Veins, thavitmay be carried back again tothe right Ventricle of the Heart; and thence by rhe Arterious Veins to the Lungs; in which after the Blood has been accended by some Nitrous Particles, breathed in thither. by the Air, it goes into the Venous Artery, thence into the left Ventricle of the Heart; which again empties it self into the Aorta, or Great Artery; so that the Body may. be nourished and enlivened, it goes into every part of it.) This is Blanchard's Account of the Matter. See more inthe Word Circulation of the Blood.

periostium.c: PERIOSTIUM, is a thin Membrane that inclosed immediately almost all the Bones in the Body, except the Teeth, Bones of the Ear, Gc. Ir hath a most exquisite Sense, and probably jis an Expansion of the Nervous and Tendinous Fibres of the Muscles. Irs use is to cover the Bones, and to sustain the Vessels which enter into them to nourish them. Dr. Havers in his Excellent Book, called, Ofteologia Nova, faith, that this Membrane consists of two forts of Fibres, of which those thar lie next the Bone, are d rived from the Dur Mater, and the others from: the Tendons of theMufcless id

peripateticks.c: PERIPATETICKS. The Chief of these was Aristotle 5 then his Successors; among whom you may reckon Theopbraftus, Cratippus, Boethius, and all his very numerous Interpreters. But about 460 Years ago, there arose a new Set of Famous Aristotelians, which were called also Peri pate. ticks; from them came the three chief Sects of: the Peripatetick Philosophy. The Tho mists stom Thomas Aquinas, who flourished 4. D. 1224. The Scotifts from Fohannes Dun Scot us, A. D. 1308. And the Nominalifts from Oc ham, who was born about 4. D. 1310. And now-a - days by the Pe vipatetick Philosophy, we understand that which was founded on the Principles of Aristotle and his Commentators and Followers; and which therefore isas frequently called, The Aristotelian Philosophy,.

peripheryingeometry.c: PERIPHERY, in Geometry, is the Circum fe - ference of a Circle, or of any other Regular Curvilineal Figure,

periphrasis.c: PERIPHRASIS, is a Citcumlocution used to avoid certain Words, whose Idea's are unpleasing; and to prevent the peaking of something that would produce ill Effects.;

peripneumonia.c: PERIPNEUMONIA, is an Inflammation of the Lungs and Breast, accompanied with a sharp Fever, hard Breathing, a Cough, and an heavy Pain. Blanchard.

perite.c: PERITE re, in Architecture, isa Place encom - round with Columns, and with kind of ings about it; here the Pillars stand without, whereas in the Peristyle they stand within.

periscii.c: PERISCII, are the Inhabitants of the two Frozen Zones, or chose that live within the Compass of the Ar tick and Antartick Circles; for as the Sun never goes down to them after he is once up, but always round about, so do their Shadows. Whence the Name.

perissology.c: PERISSOLOGY, is a Discourse silled up with unnecessary and superfluous Words.

peristaltickmotion.c: PERISTALTICK Motion, isa Vermicular or Wormlike Motion of the Intestines, whereby the Excrements are voided. Also the Motions of the Vessels, whereby Humours, as Water, Chyle, the rey &c. ascend and descend, is sometimes so called.

peristiphalinus.c: PERISTIPHALINUS, internus & externus, are Muscles of the Uvxla, the one pulling it forwards, and the other backwards.

peristyleinarchite.c: PERISTYLE, in Archite & ure, is a Place or Building encompass'd with Pillars, standing round about within the Court: But this Word Peristyle is sometimes taken for a Row or Rank of Columns, as well without as within any Edifice; as in Cloyfters and Galleries: Sometimes this was called Anti prostyle.

peritonzaun.c: PERITONZAUN, is a Membrane ( of an Oval Figure) which clothes the whole Abdomen on the Inside, and its Entrails on the Outside: It consists of two Tunicks, and adheres above tothe Diaphragma, below to the Os Ilium; before to the Transverse Muscles, but chiefly to their Tendons about the Linea Alba; behind, it grows to the Fleshy Heads of these Muscles.

peritrochiuminmechanicks.c: PERITROCHIUM, in Mechanicks is a kind of Wheel, or Circular Frame of Wood, placed somewhere upon an Axis, or Cylinder, round which a Rope is wound, in order to raise a Weight; and the Use of this Perstrochium, is to make the Cylinder or Axis berurned the more easily by the Means of Stayes or Levers, which are six'd in its Circumference. See Axis in Peritrochio, 7

perjury.c: PERJURY, is a Crime committed, when a lawful Oath is ministered by any that hath Authority, to any Persons in any Judicial Proceedings; who wear absolutely and falfly ina Matter material to the Issue or Cause in Question, either of their own Accord, or by the Subordination of others. Note, If a Man call me Perjured Man, 1 may have my Action upon the Cafe; but for calling me a Forsworn Man, no Action lies, And Perjury is excepted out of the Act of General Pardon.

permeating.c: PERMEATING, is penetrating into, and sing thro the Pores of any Body. Mr. Boyle a Smoak ing Liquor, which he called, The Pereme ating Menstruum, and its Operations, The Pene trant, or Permeating Fumes, It was made of equal parts of Flos Sulpburis, Sal Armoniack, and good Quick Lime, all powdered, and well mingled together, and then distilled by Degrees of Fire in a Retort, " till the Sand which contains the Retort, become almost red-hot; for then will come over a Liquor which will be continual! soaking, and consequently must be kept well stop'd. With this Fuming Liquor he made several Experiments to evince the Porosity of Bodies 5 by discovering, that tho Coins, ce. were wrap'd up close in Leather, &c. yet the Fumes of this Permeating Menstruum would ger thro them, and cis colour the Metal. Vid. Essay of Porosity of Body, p. 36, 37 fie eidem annexed cum Ecclefi 2 & prebenda, is a Writ to an Ordinary, commanding him to admit a Clerk to a Benefice, upon Exchange made with another,; PER my & cbr in Law, a Joint-Tenant is said to be seized of the Lands that he holds jointly Per my & per tout; that is, he is seised by every Parcel, and by the whole.

psoasparvus.c: - PSOAS Parvus, is a Muscle of the Thigh, which arises fleshy from the superior part of the first Vertebra of the Loins, internally and laterally within the Abdomen, immediately below the Cavity of the Diaphragm, whence descending obliquely inwards towards the Pelvis Abdominis ( where it ceases ro be fleshy) in a Manner embracing the P / oas magnus, and is inferred with a thin broad strong Tendon, to that Part of the Os Pubis, where it is join'd to the Os Wi um: This Muscle with its Partner acting, assists the Re ti Abdominis in drawing the ossa pubis upwards, 4 s in raising ourselves from a decumbent Posture. Thus Rope - dancers hang by their hands, and raise the inferior parts of their Bodies to take Kold of a Rope with their Feet. pannagepannaginm.c: PANNAGE, Pannaginm; signified formerly both the running and feeding of Hogs within a Foreft, and also the Price that was paid for their so running. Pannagium Liberum, or Free Pan wage, was a Liberty of free running for Swine within the Limits'of such Forests or Woods; and Was sometimes a Privilege granted to some private Persons, and to several Religious Houses. this Pannage were not duely paid, there was a Process from the Exchequer and a De straint by the Sheriff. The Title of Pannage was sometimes alienated from the Parith Priest to the Appropriators. Dr. Kennet's Paroch. Antiq. i

pressure.c: PRESSURE; by this Word some Philosophers, ee ee addicted ro the Cartesian Hypothesis, mean a ki of Motion which is impressed and ny) through a Fluid Miadiden:: And by this deerwrauld explain all the Phenomena of Light and Colours, as well as of many other BE 3 by certain new Modifications. which do there happen to the Rays of Light, as they are usually called. But as our Excellent Sir If. Newton thews, ( p. 307 of the Latin Edition of his Opticks) this is a Mistake. For if Light ( for Instance) consisted only it Pressure, propagated without Actual Motion, it could not therefore agitate and warm such -. dies as Refle & t and Refract it: And if it consisted in an Instantaneous Motion, or one propagated ta all Distances in an Instant; as ome have advanced; there would be required an Infinite vfs or, Force, to produce that Motion, every Moment, in every Lucent Particle. And if Light consisted either in Pressure, or in Motion propagated in a Fluid Medium, whether instantaneously or in Time, it must from thence come to pass, that it should inflect itself in umbram. For Pressure or Motion in a Fluid Medium cannot be propagated in Right Lines, beyond any Obstacle which shall hinder any Part of the Motion; but will inflect and diffuse ic self every Way into those Parcs of the Quiescent Medium which lie beyond the said Obstacle. Thus the Force of Gravity tends downward, but the Pressure, which arises from that Force of Gravity tends every Way with an Equable Force: And with equal Ease and Force, is propagated in Crooked Lines as in Straight.. Waves on the Surface of Water while they slide by the Sides of any Large Obstacle, do inflect, dilate and disease themselves by Degrees, into the Quiescent Water lying beyond the Obstacle. The Waves, Pulses, or Vibrations of our Air in which Sounds consist, do manifestly isle t themselves, tho not so much as the Waves of Water; for the Sound of a Bell or of a Cannon, can be heard over a Hill, which intercepts the Sonorous Object from our sight: And Sounds will be propagated as easily thro Crooked Tubes, as thro, Straight: But Light is never observed to go in Curve Lines nor to inflect it elf in Umbram, For the fixed Stars do immediately disappear on the Interposition of any of the Planets, as well as some Parts of the Suns Body, by the Interposition of the Moon, Venus or Mercury.
